'''''Galinsoga parviflora'''''<ref>[http://www.rnzih.org.nz/pages/weednameslist.htm   Royal New Zealand Institute of Horticulture – Horticulture Pages – Weeds – Index of names]</ref> is a species of [[herbaceous plant]] in the daisy [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Asteraceae]]. It has several common names including '''guasca''' (Colombia), '''pacpa yuyo''', '''paco yuyo''', and '''waskha''' (Peru), '''burrionera''' (Ecuador), '''albahaca silvestre''' and '''saetilla''' (Argentina), '''mielcilla''' (Costa Rica), '''piojito''' ([[Oaxaca|Oaxaca, Mexico]]), '''galinsoga''' (New Zealand), '''gallant soldier''',<ref name="BSBI07">{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}</ref><ref name="PLANTS">{{PLANTS|id=GAPA2|taxon=Galinsoga parviflora|accessdate=19 January 2016}}</ref> '''quickweed''',<ref name="PLANTS" /> and '''potato weed''' (United Kingdom, United States).

==History==
''Galinsoga parviflora'' was brought from [[Peru]] to [[Kew Gardens]] in 1796, and later escaped to the wild in [[Great Britain]] and [[Ireland]], being temporarily known as the 'Kew Weed'.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Flora Britannica: supported by common ground|last1=Mabey|first1=Richard|last2=Lovett Jones|first2=Gareth|last3=Gibbons|first3=Bob|publisher=Chatto & Windus|isbn=1-85619-377-2|oclc=805221553|year = 1996}}</ref> The plant is named after the Spanish botanist [[Ignacio Mariano Martinez de Galinsoga]]. The species name '''parviflora''<nowiki/>' translates to 'having small flowers'.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Plant names explained: botanical terms and their meaning|first=Sue|last=Gordon|date=2007-01-01|publisher=David & Charles|isbn=978-0-7153-2188-1|oclc=471017850}}</ref> In Britain, its name ''Galinsoga'' is sometimes popularly rendered as "gallant soldiers", and then sometimes altered to "soldiers of the Queen". In Malawi, where the plant is naturalised, it is known as 'Mwamuna aligone' which translates to 'My husband is sleeping'.<ref name=":0" />

==Description==
''Galinsoga parviflora'' grows to a height of {{cvt|75|cm|in|-1}}. It is a branched herb with opposite stalked leaves, toothed at the margins. The flowers are in small heads. The 3–8 white ray-florets are about {{convert|10|mm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}} long and 3-lobed. The central disc florets are yellow and tubular.<ref>Clapham, A.R., Tutin, T.G. and Warburg, E.F. 1968 ''Excursion Flora of the British Isles.'' Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|0-521-04656-4}}</ref><ref name="x">[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200023969 Flora of China, ''Galinsoga parviflora'' Cavanilles, 1795. <big>牛膝菊</big> niu xi ju]</ref>

==Identification==
Gallant soldier is usually more-or-less [[Glabrousness|glabrous]], whereas the otherwise similar [[Galinsoga quadriradiata|shaggy soldier]] tends to be very hairy, but these characters are insufficient for accurate identification. To be confident, it is important to check (with a hand lens) that gallant soldier has three-pointed tips to the scales on the [[Receptacle (botany)|receptacle]], and scales in the [[Pappus (botany)|pappus]] with smooth margins and a blunt point at the top.<ref name=Stace>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |location=Suffolk |publisher=C&M Floristics |edition=4th |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref>
[[File:Galinsoga parviflora var. semicalva - Flickr - aspidoscelis.jpg|thumb|none|The pappus scales have smooth (not hairy) margins and a blunt tip.]]

==Distribution==
The species is native to South America; however, it is widely naturalized in other countries.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.brc.ac.uk/plantatlas/index.php?q=plant/galinsoga-parviflora|title=Galinsoga parviflora (Gallant-soldier) {{!}} Online Atlas of the British and Irish Flora|website=www.brc.ac.uk|language=en|access-date=2017-05-16}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | url=http://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/25299 | title=Galinsoga parviflora (Gallant soldier) | date=2014 | doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.25299 | last1=Rojas-Sandoval | first1=J. | last2=Acevedo-Rodríguez | first2=P. | journal=CABI Compendium | volume=CABI Compendium | article-number=25299 | doi-access=free }}</ref> There are a few records of ''G. parviflora'' and ''[[Galinsoga quadriradiata|G. quadriradiata]]'' in [[Northern Ireland]].<ref>Hackney, P. (Ed.) 1992. ''Stewart & Corry's Flora of the North-east of Ireland''. Third Edition. {{ISBN|0-85389-446-9}}</ref> It has been naturalized elsewhere, including North America and Australasia.<ref>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=200023969 Flora of North America, ''Galinsoga parviflora'' Cavanilles, 1795.]</ref><ref name="x" /><ref>[http://bie.ala.org.au/species/Galinsoga+parviflora Atlas of Living Australia]</ref><ref>[http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=galinsoga+parviflora Altervista Flora Italiana, ''Galinsoga parviflora'' Cav.] includes photos, European distribution map</ref>{{Excessive citations inline|date=September 2021}}

==Uses==
In Colombia it is used as a herb in the soup ''[[ajiaco]]''.<ref name="s">[http://www.b-and-t-world-seeds.com/86392.html B & T World Seeds, ''Tridax parviflora (Galinsoga parviflora)'' in Profile] includes photo plus recipe for soup containing this plant as an ingredient</ref> In Oaxaca, Mexico, it is used as an ingredient in ''[[sopa de guías]]'', a soup made from squash vines, fresh corn and wild herbs. It can also be used as an ingredient in leaf salads, although its subtle flavour, reminiscent of artichoke, mostly develops after being cooked. In eastern Africa, the plant is collected from the wild, and its leaves, stem and flowers eaten. It is also dried and ground into powder for use in soups.<ref>{{cite book |editor1-last= Prance |editor1-first=Ghillean |editor2-last=Nesbitt |editor2-first=Mark |last1=Pieroni |first1=Andrea |author-link=Andrea Pieroni (ethnobotanist) |date=2005 |title=The Cultural History of Plants |publisher=Routledge |page=31 |isbn=0-415-92746-3}}</ref>

== Phytochemicals ==
In ''G. parviflora'', the major [[phytochemical]]s are [[phenolic acid]]s, [[depside]]s and [[flavonoid]]s with their corresponding [[glycoside]]s.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Skarupova |first1=Denisa |last2=Vostalova |first2=Jitka |last3=Rajnochova Svobodova |first3=Alena |date=2020-03-26 |title=Ultraviolet A protective potential of plant extracts and phytochemicals |journal=Biomedical Papers |language=en |volume=164 |issue=1 |pages=1–22 |doi=10.5507/bp.2020.010|pmid=32188958 |doi-access=free }}</ref> The flavonoids present are patulitrin, quercimeritrin, [[quercetagetin]], [[luteolin]] 7-β-D-glucopyranoside, apigenin 7-β-D-glucoside, galinsoside A, galinsoside B, 7,3',4'-trihydroxyflavanone and 3,5,7,3',4'-pentahydroxyflavanone. Phenolic acids and depsides includes [[vanillic acid]], isovanillic acid, [[P-Coumaric acid|p-coumaric acid]], [[P-Hydroxybenzoic acid|p-hydroxybenzoic acid]], o-hydroxyphenyl acetic acid, [[caffeic acid]], [[chlorogenic acid]] and caffeoylglucaric acids.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Parzonko |first1=Andrzej |last2=Kiss |first2=Anna K. |date=17 Dec 2018 |title=Caffeic acid derivatives isolated from Galinsoga parviflora herb protected human dermal fibroblasts from UVA-radiation |journal=Phytomedicine: International Journal of Phytotherapy and Phytopharmacology |volume=57 |pages=215–222 |doi=10.1016/j.phymed.2018.12.022 |issn=1618-095X |pmid=30785017|s2cid=73505361 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Studzińska-Sroka |first1=Elżbieta |last2=Dudek-Makuch |first2=Marlena |last3=Chanaj-Kaczmarek |first3=Justyna |last4=Czepulis |first4=Natasza |last5=Korybalska |first5=Katarzyna |last6=Rutkowski |first6=Rafał |last7=Łuczak |first7=Joanna |last8=Grabowska |first8=Karolina |last9=Bylka |first9=Wiesława |last10=Witowski |first10=Janusz |date=24 August 2018 |title=Anti-inflammatory Activity and Phytochemical Profile of Galinsoga Parviflora Cav. |journal=Molecules |language=en |volume=23 |issue=9 |page=2133 |doi=10.3390/molecules23092133 |pmid=30149540 |pmc=6225198 |issn=1420-3049|doi-access=free }}</ref>
